title: 08. Multi-Agent & Patterns: Day 13 — RAG Agents
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the pattern behind every "chat with your docs" product.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the pattern behind every "chat with your docs" product. The recipe is simple: chunk your documents, embed each chunk, store the embeddings in a vector database, then for each user query retrieve the top-k most similar chunks and stuff them into the LLM prompt as context. Today you build two RAG agents with two different framings.

1. **Personal Doc RAG** (LangChain) — uses ChromaDB as a persistent vector store, OpenAI embeddings, and an LCEL retriever chain. This is the "classic" RAG pipeline.
2. **Slack History Searcher** (Pydantic AI) — wraps a custom TF-IDF retriever as an `@agent.tool`. The agent decides when to retrieve, how many results to fetch, and how to cite them. This is "RAG-as-tool," which works better when retrieval should be optional or conditional.

The contrast matters: a chain always retrieves (good for "answer only from these docs"), a tool retrieves on demand (good for "answer from these docs when relevant, otherwise use your own knowledge").

sections.title: Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
**Chunk size too large or too small.** A 2,000-character chunk means each chunk covers too much ground and similarity scores become noisy. A 100-character chunk means each chunk is too thin to be self-contained. The sweet spot for most prose is 400-800 characters with 10-20% overlap. Experiment with your own docs — `chunk_size` is a tunable, not a constant.

**Forgetting to deduplicate on re-ingest.** If you run `vs.add_documents(chunks)` twice, Chroma stores two copies of every chunk. The retriever will then return duplicates, wasting context tokens. Either clear the collection first (`vs.delete_collection()`) or use deterministic document IDs and upsert.

**Embedding costs add up fast.** `text-embedding-3-small` is cheap but not free. A 10,000-document corpus at ~500 tokens per doc is ~5M tokens = $0.10 per full re-embedding. That's fine once. But if you re-embed on every code change during development, you'll burn through credits. Use `persist_directory` and only re-embed when documents actually change.

**Citations that don't match the source.** LLMs sometimes invent source filenames or attribute a claim to the wrong chunk. Two mitigations: (1) make source labels unambiguous (`[source: quarterly_report.txt chunk 3 of 7]`), (2) post-process the answer to verify every cited source actually appears in the retrieved chunks. For high-stakes use cases, use a structured output schema that forces citations as a separate field.

**Tool RAG models that refuse to call the tool.** If the system prompt is weak, the model will sometimes answer from its training data instead of retrieving. Fix with explicit instructions: "Always call search_slack at least once before answering. If the tool returns no results, say so." You can also enforce this structurally by chaining the retriever into the prompt (the chain RAG pattern from Project 1).

**TF-IDF vs dense embeddings.** TF-IDF (Project 2) is keyword-based — it doesn't understand synonyms. "Deploy blocked" won't match a message saying "release is stuck." Dense embeddings (Project 1) handle synonyms but cost money and require an embedding model. For small, well-defined vocabularies (Slack channels with consistent jargon), TF-IDF can be surprisingly competitive. For general documents, use embeddings.

sections.title: Next: Day 14 — Streaming & UX
sections.body: Everything you've built so far returns the full answer at once. Real products stream: you see the email being typed token-by-token, the meeting summary appearing section by section. Tomorrow you build a Live Email Drafter with LangChain + `rich.live`, and a Real-time Meeting Summarizer with Pydantic AI's `agent.iter()` that prints every event in the agent loop as it happens. These UX patterns are what make agents feel alive.
